problems.title: Two Sum
hints: A brute-force solution checks every pair with two nested loops in O(N^2). Can you do better?
Can you use a Hash Map to store numbers you have already visited and check for the complement in O(1) time?
problems.description:
Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to `target`.

You may assume that each input would have **exactly one solution**, and you may not use the same element twice.

You can return the answer in any order.

constraints: `s` consists only of printable ASCII characters.
Optimal space complexity: O(1) using two pointers

examples.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

examples.explanation: An empty string reads the same forward and backward.

testCases.input: "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

problems.description:
A phrase is a **palindrome** if, after converting all uppercase letters into lowercase letters and removing all non-alphanumeric characters, it reads the same forward and backward. Alphanumeric characters include letters and numbers.

Given a string `s`, return `true` if it is a palindrome, or `false` otherwise.
hints: Consider two pointers starting at the beginning and the end of the string.
Increment the left pointer and decrement the right pointer until both point to alphanumeric characters.

problems.description: Given an integer array `nums`, return `true` if any value appears **at least twice** in the array, and return `false` if every element is distinct.

examples.explanation:
nums[0] + nums[1] + nums[2] = (-1) + 0 + 1 = 0.
nums[1] + nums[2] + nums[4] = 0 + 1 + (-1) = 0.
nums[0] + nums[3] + nums[4] = (-1) + 2 + (-1) = 0.
The distinct triplets are [-1,0,1] and [-1,-1,2].

hints: Sorting the array first makes it easy to avoid duplicate triplets and enables the two-pointer technique.
Fix the first element nums[i] and use two pointers (left and right) to find pairs that sum to -nums[i].
problems.description:
Given an integer array `nums`, return all the triplets `[nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]]` such that `i != j`, `i != k`, and `j != k`, and `nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0`.

Notice that the solution set must not contain duplicate triplets.

hints: Use the sliding window technique with two pointers [left, right].

examples.explanation: The answer is "abc", with the length of 3.

constraints: `s` consists of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces.

problems.title: Group Anagrams
hints: Two words are anagrams if and only if their sorted character representations are identical.
problems.description:
Given an array of strings `strs`, group the **anagrams** together. You can return the answer in **any order**.

An Anagram is a word or phrase formed by rearranging the letters of a different word or phrase, typically using all the original letters exactly once.

problems.title: Trapping Rain Water
problems.description: Given `n` non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is `1`, compute how much water it can trap after raining.
hints: For each element, how much water can be trapped above it? It is min(maxLeft, maxRight) - currentHeight.
Can you maintain maxLeft and maxRight dynamically using two pointers moving inwards?
constraints: Optimal time: O(N), Optimal space: O(1)

examples.explanation: The elevation map traps 6 units of rain water.

problems.title: Coin Change
hints: Think of this as finding the shortest path in a graph where nodes are amounts from 0 to amount.
Define dp[i] as the minimum coins needed to make amount i. What is the transition relation?
problems.description:
You are given an integer array `coins` representing coins of different denominations and an integer `amount` representing a total amount of money.

Return the **fewest number of coins** that you need to make up that amount. If that amount of money cannot be made up by any combination of the coins, return `-1`.

You may assume that you have an infinite number of each kind of coin.

hints: Model the courses and prerequisites as a Directed Graph.

problems.description:
There are a total of `numCourses` courses you have to take, labeled from `0` to `numCourses - 1`. You are given an array `prerequisites` where `prerequisites[i] = [a_i, b_i]` indicates that you **must** take course `b_i` first if you want to take course `a_i`.

Return `true` if you can finish all courses. Otherwise, return `false` (i.e. if there is a circular dependency / cycle).

problems.title: Valid Parentheses String with Wildcards
problems.description:
Given a string `s` containing only three types of characters: '(', ')' and '*', return true if `s` is valid.

Rules:
1. Any left parenthesis '(' must have a corresponding right parenthesis ')'.
2. Any right parenthesis ')' must have a corresponding left parenthesis '('.
3. Left parenthesis '(' must go before the corresponding right parenthesis ')'.
4. '*' could be treated as a single right parenthesis ')' or a single left parenthesis '(' or an empty string "".
hints: Consider tracking the minimum and maximum possible count of open parentheses as you iterate through the string.
When encountering a ')', decrease both counts. When encountering a '*', minCount decreases (acting as ')') and maxCount increases (acting as '(').
If maxCount becomes negative at any moment, return false immediately.

problems.description: Given an array of sorted integers, find target index in O(log n).

improvements: Transition from an O(n^2) brute-force approach to an O(n) approach using a Hash Map to store visited values.
Consider early input validation to ensure the input array has at least two elements.
Adopt modern JavaScript best practices like using 'const' for variables that do not require re-assignment.
aiReview.timeComplexity: O(n^2) where n is the number of elements in the array, due to the nested loops comparing each pair of elements.
aiReview.suggestedOptimizedSnippet: function twoSum(nums, target) { const map = new Map(); for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) { const complement = target - nums[i]; if (map.has(complement)) return [map.get(complement), i]; map.set(nums[i], i); } return []; }
aiReview.spaceComplexity: O(1) because the solution only uses a fixed amount of extra space for loop variables regardless of the input size.
edgeCasesCovered: Target values reachable by the first and last elements.
aiReview.summary: Your solution is logically sound and correctly solves the problem by checking every possible pair. While it satisfies the requirements, it is computationally inefficient for large datasets. In professional environments, we prioritize O(n) solutions using Hash Maps to avoid redundant iterations.
edgeCasesMissed: Large input arrays where O(n^2) complexity will lead to performance bottlenecks.
Empty or single-element arrays (though the problem guarantees a solution, defensive programming is recommended).
strengths: Clean, readable implementation following standard iteration patterns.
Correctly handles the requirement to return indices without reusing the same element.
Effective use of early return to terminate as soon as the solution is found.

messages.text: Welcome to CodeElevate Academy! Our AI Mentor is online 24/7 in your coding playground. Feel free to ask questions here or use the "Ask AI Tutor" side drawer while solving.
Has anyone tackled the Trapping Rain Water problem yet? I found that using two pointers was much easier than maintaining two separate prefix/suffix maximum arrays.
Spot on, Alex! The two-pointer approach reduces the space complexity from O(N) to O(1) by lazily evaluating whichever boundary is strictly smaller.
